blocks.text: But I can scarcely believe that Bochart has established anything certain by this whole very learned discussion. Let us weigh the force of his arguments. One will look in vain in this entire chapter for any explicit statement of them. At the very outset he assumes that עגור is the crane, but he is completely silent about the reasons that led him to it. Yet, so far as one can gather from the course of the whole discussion, he seems to have reasoned thus: "From the two passages of Isaiah and Jeremiah it is clear that עגור is a migratory bird and one using a strained voice; and we find both of these in the crane; therefore עגור is the crane." Nothing would be more certain than this, if those two features were peculiar to cranes. As it is, since there are many migratory birds that use a strained voice, you see how unsafe this argument is unless weightier ones are added. But Bochart is wholly without these, so that there is not even one of the ancients on whose authority he can safely rely. For the Syriac and the Chaldee put crane where the Hebrew text has סוס, but swallow in place of עגור; unless you say that the words have been transposed in both translators, which Bochart assumes without any adequate reason, merely in favour of his preconceived opinion. Equally weak is the other argument for the crane, drawn from the fact that the Arabic عجر [ʿjr] means he returned; for on that basis all migratory birds whatsoever could have been so named. But what chiefly restrains me from taking עגור as the name of the crane is this: that in Isaiah chirping (צפצף) is attributed to the birds סוס and עגור. — VELTHUSEN (in Symbolae Kilonienses vol. 2, p. 273—390) labours hard to show that the Hebrew עגור is the same word as نغر [nughar], the Arabic name of the nightingale, with an interchange of ن and ע (whose related sound in pronunciation once approached ng, like the French n in mon, ton), and of ג and غ, examples of whose interchange Schultens gives in the Clavis Dialectorum p. 199. He further argues that the nightingale was in the minds both of the Alexandrians, when they put στρουθια [strouthia], sparrows, in Jeremiah, that bird being of their kind; and of the Chaldee and the Syriac, who in their Jeremiah by כורכיא (from the verb כָּרַךְ to cover) would indicate a bird that hides itself amid thick foliage in mourning, i.e. the nightingale, and by that word sought at the same time to express the same notion of hiding in the verb עגר that can be derived from the Arabic عجر [ʿjr], in Conjugation 5 he covered himself. How contrived and far-fetched all this is, anyone will easily notice for himself. — EVERARD SCHEIDIUS, in his Dissertatio ad Canticum Hiskiae p. 86 ff., taking our עגור in Isaiah as a passive participle of the verb עגר, which, on the testimony of Giauhari and Firuzabadi, has the notion of twisting and bending, considers it an epithet of the swallow, which, struck with fear, wheels this way and that and repeatedly turns aside in its course. — Paulus too, in the Clavis to Isaiah, took the word for a participle; but since he there regards סוס as the name of the horse (cf. note 4 to the preceding Chapter), he interprets עגור as disturbed, anxious, calling to his aid the Syriac ܥܓܘܪܐ and also the Arabic عجر [ʿjr], to turn aside in the way, to wheel, so that the poet, tossed by the heat of fever, compares himself with an exhausted horse, panting from the depths of its chest and uttering a shrill and sharp sound, which is expressed by the verb [II, 632] צפצף. — To me עגור seems to be the name of a bird in Isaiah too, chiefly for this reason: that in Ierem. VIII, 7. the same words סיס and עגור are joined, and joined in such a way that it is evident that עגור is the name of a bird, like תור and סיס, which precede. But which species of bird is meant, since the other dialects are silent and the ancients disagree remarkably, no one today can say.
